On Thursday night, Pakistan attacked targets in Afghanistan. The results of that attack are disputed. The Taliban, the Islamic fundamentalist nationalist movement that controls Afghanistan, says that between nine and 10 civilians were killed, including women and children. But Pakistan claims the strike killed 22 militants and destroyed weapons and ammunition depots.
These early October attacks are just the latest escalation in a conflict between the two countries that reignited mid-September, after months of comparative calm.

The conflict was sparked again after a series of attacks on Pakistani security forces. On September 18, an attack on a police compound in the northwestern city of Kohat resulted in the deaths of 31 people and more than 100 injured. A splinter group belonging to the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, claimed responsibility for the attack in Kohat, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, bordering Afghanistan.
Pakistan accused Afghanistan of providing the TTP with a safe haven. Afghanistan denies this but clashes at the border and then airstrikes by Pakistan followed.

The TTP in Pakistan is not the same as Afghanistan's Taliban. Although it does have close ideological and personnel ties to the Afghan Taliban, it is an independent organization that fights the Pakistani state.

Many of its fighters sided with the Taliban during that country's long-running insurgency against international and US troops. This is why, after the Taliban returned to power in 2021, the TTP gained more room and more leverage. This has meant that Afghanistan — a former ally of Pakistan — has increasingly become a threat to its neighbor.
Pakistan has asked the Taliban to take action against the TTP, but the close connection between the two make this difficult.

"Because of these personal connections and networks, it is extremely difficult for the Afghan Taliban to break away," says Conrad Schetter, director of the Bonn International Center for Conflict Studies, or BICC.

The connections don't mean that the Taliban has any control over the TTP. There are certainly historical connections between the two, but Schetter doesn't believe that equals any sort of strong, direct influence.

"The Taliban are simply not prepared to take orders from Islamabad," adds Thomas Ruttig, co-director of the Afghanistan Analysts Network, a think tank working between Kabul and Berlin. "They won't let anyone outside interfere."
This means the Pakistani policy of supporting the Taliban in order to gain influence in Afghanistan hasn't worked.

There's also another older conflict that has an impact on the current situation. This involves what is known as the Durand Line, drawn in 1893 by a British diplomat and an Afghan emir to mark spheres of influence between British India and Afghanistan.

The current border between Afghanistan and Pakistan follows the Durand Line and also divides an area on both sides, homeland to Pashtuns, who make up the largest ethnic group in Afghanistan and second largest in Pakistan.
So the border dispute here isn't just about territory, it's also about identity.
"Ethnic and nationalist elements play a significant role in the conflict," Schetter tells DW. Many Pashtuns still refuse to accept the border that the Durand Line created.

In Pakistan, the country's long-running rivalry with India also plays a part. A friendly Afghanistan would have been advantageous for Pakistan. But India has also strengthened its ties to the Taliban.

"While Islamabad once viewed Afghanistan as a source of 'strategic depth' in its rivalry with India, it now increasingly views its north-western neighbor as a liability," an analysis by British think tank Chatham House notes.

Pakistan still has power over Afghanistan, though. As a landlocked country, Afghanistan relies on trade routes through neighboring countries, and Pakistan in particular. Pakistan can use border closures and trade restrictions to exert pressure even as the Taliban regime is trying to reduce dependence on Pakistan and find new economic and political partners.

Trade and security considerations are now becoming tangled. Pakistan has held talks with the TTP that were mediated by the Taliban and ceasefires were agreed upon. Talks between Pakistan and Afghanistan also took place. But none of the temporary agreements resolved the crucial question of how to prevent attacks on Pakistan from Afghan territory.

So in parallel with diplomacy, Pakistan has also been relying on economic and political pressure, for example, by closing borders and restricting trade and by sending Afghan refugees back into Afghanistan.

An analysis by the US-based Council on Foreign Relations notes that the Taliban are worried that if they crack down on the TTP too hard, they will drive the group towards another extremist militant group, the Islamic State in Khorasan Province or IS-K. This group opposes the Taliban.

The conflict recently escalated to another level. At the end of September, Kabul reported 28 killed and 32 captured fighters who had infiltrated Afghanistan from Nuristan province, Pakistan. The Taliban accused Pakistan of supporting its armed opponents, something Pakistan has denied.

"It is known from past decades that Pakistan has regularly supported armed groups on the Afghan side — for example, the Mujahideen during the Soviet occupation and later the Taliban," Ruttig points out. "What's new though is that Pakistan apparently also supports parts of today's armed anti-Taliban opposition."
This is turning the dispute over the TTP into a larger conflict in which both sides accuse each other of supporting armed groups from the other's territory.

British think tank Chatham House speaks of a significant escalation compared to previous border skirmishes. Worryingly, a conflict over armed groups and border incidents is turning into a direct confrontation between the two nation states.
Ruttig believes that it would be possible to contain the spiraling violence if both sides return to negotiations.

"If both sides were willing to return to the negotiating table — perhaps with international mediation —there would be ways to contain the conflict and, above all, to protect the civilian population on both sides," he argues.

In a late September commentary in Pakistani weekly magazine The Friday Times, Pakistani analyst Saqib Ali Khan advocates for several things that could ease the tensions. That includes a reliable channel between Islamabad and Kabul, a separate approach for armed groups and greater involvement of the population along the border.
The conflict, he argues, is not merely a dispute between two governments but also a security, border, economic and regional conflict.
"Along those lines, there would have to be a shift in perspective on both sides," Schetter concludes.
In the long term, greater economic integration is also needed, he adds, so that Pakistan and Afghanistan do not define their relationship solely through security and power issues.

Two Iranian nationals charged with plotting acts of terrorism against the United Kingdom's Jewish community were remanded in custody by a court in London on Saturday.
The pair were detained on September 20, the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.
The case only came to light on Friday when the two men were charged, just days after another terror plot, which the UK has linked to Iran, was foiled.

Prosecutor Mark Luckett told Westminster Magistrates' Court that Rahman S., 34, and Salam A., 36, are accused of carrying out "hostile reconnaissance" on Jewish targets in Manchester, northern England.
He said the two men planned to use a "homemade explosive device" and had allegedly been in contact with a third party, an Iranian national, most likely operating from within Iran.
The contact is alleged to have given the pair instructions on how to put together a homemade device from chlorine and brake fluid, the court heard.
Luckett said the two suspects had used online resources, including images, plans and maps, to identify and research potential attack sites.
He told the court that the targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and the Heaton Park synagogue, where two Jewish worshippers were killed in a knife attack a year ago on Friday.
The two Iranian suspects had arrived in Britain in small boats that crossed the English Channel from mainland Europe, Luckett added.
One had been granted asylum, while the other's application is still pending, the court heard.
The pair did not enter a plea and were remanded in custody until their next hearing at London's Old Bailey on October 23.
Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator of counterterror policing, said the plot was believed to be isolated and there was no ongoing public threat.
Police find no link to RAF Fairford plot

Evans also said the Manchester plot was "not connected in any way" to the suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford last weekend, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham said showed "strong indications" of Iranian involvement.
Also on Saturday, police said a dual British-Iranian national, arrested on Thursday in connection with the RAF Fairford plot, was released on police bail.
The 25-year-old was the sixth person arrested and then bailed as the investigation continues.
Police said the five other men held are all British nationals in their 20s and from London.

Police uncovered the RAF Fairford plot when a farmer spotted suspicious white vans near the base early on Sunday morning and called the authorities. Officers found petrol inside the vans, but no explosives.
UK media reported this week that one of the suspects dialled the police about an hour earlier, though that has not been confirmed.
Tehran has rejected as baseless accusations of targeting RAF Fairford, which lies 90 miles (145 kilometers) west of London and has been used by US bombers to strike Iran.
The UK remains on high alert for potential threats from Russia and Iran.
Iran has previously used proxies to commit crimes on British soil, including repeated attacks and plots against Jewish targets, as well as against dissidents.
Antisemitic attacks more broadly have risen sharply since Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023.

Cornell president calls alleged gang rape 'deeply disturbing,' pledges greater transparency
Michael Kotlikoff addressed Cornell community in 8-minute video message

Cornell University's president called the alleged gang rape of a student at a fraternity house in 2024 "deeply disturbing" on Saturday, saying it would weigh on the school for years to come and pledging greater transparency amid mounting outrage over the university's purported handling of the case.

In an eight-minute video message to the Cornell community, Michael Kotlikoff described the past week as one of the most difficult in the university's history and acknowledged troubling questions about the investigations that followed the allegations.

"My heart aches when I think of what she experienced," Kotlikoff said. "It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use."

Kotlikoff reaffirmed his commitment to supporting an independent review of Cornell's handling of the case called for by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and said the school's board of trustees would announce details next week. He also expressed support for Hochul's decision to turn the criminal investigation over to the state attorney general.

"I want to acknowledge something that can be difficult for an institution to say," Kotlikoff said. "We don't have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves."

Scrutiny has mounted in recent days over Cornell's response to allegations that the woman was sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members in 2024. The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, has sued the university and seven former students.

During a student assembly hearing Thursday that gave students an opportunity to voice concerns and discuss proposals to improve Cornell's response to sexual assault, several speakers called for Kotlikoff's resignation.

Hochul, asked at a news conference Friday whether she believed Kotlikoff should resign over the university's handling of the case, declined to take a position, saying she did not yet have enough information.

Kotlikoff acknowledged frustration that Cornell has not communicated enough, saying that has led to distrust. While citing "real legal and privacy limits" on what the university can disclose, he pledged greater transparency and more opportunities for students, parents and others to engage with university leaders.
He also committed Cornell's support to legislative efforts to change New York's sexual assault laws.

The case has renewed scrutiny of a state law that makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults involving people who voluntarily consume alcohol or drugs, even if they became too intoxicated to consent.

Tompkins County district attorney Matthew Van Houten cited the law in defending his initial decision not to pursue charges, saying the woman's original statement to police described voluntary drug use and sexual activity.

Critics have long sought to close what they call the "voluntary intoxication loophole," which distinguishes between people incapacitated by drugs administered without their consent and those who voluntarily became intoxicated. Hochul has pledged to push for changes to the law.

Kotlikoff also called for a "serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life," saying Cornell would engage students, alumni and others in examining how to preserve the benefits of Greek life while strengthening accountability and transparency.
"Being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility for our own actions, for how we treat others or for speaking up when someone may be at risk," he said.

Antonelli further stretched his lead over teammate Russell from 66 points to 84, with seven races remaining on the schedule, including those in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

It is easy, when you’re not of a Novocastrian persuasion, to say they lost no admirers, or that they did themselves proud.
Such words are of cold comfort in the quiet void of defeat, and truth doesn’t always cut through the pain.
But it is still important to say it, because there is still honour to be had, and they earned that with their effort and their toughness and their ability to save at least half a dozen tries.

When Kalyn Ponga went the length of the field midway through the first half, completing a play where he started out making a try-saving tackle on Billy Smith in one corner and finished scoring in the other, running about as far as a person can on a rugby league field, it felt like the moment that would last forever from this match.

The gut-busting effort to cover so much ground in the first place, the long journey towards the very heart of the Newcastle fans who had turned Stadium Australia into a little piece of the Hunter and the fact that the Knights had, yet again, scored from a thousand miles out gave a feeling that maybe this really was destiny.

Those tries from the ends of the Earth have been Newcastle’s hammer of the gods through this finals run, but in the second half the Roosters gave them no Earth to run from because the Tricolours were as inevitable as the tide through the middle of the field.
They tried to starve the Knights to death and just about did it.
Newcastle had six tackles inside the opposition all night compared to 51 for the Roosters as the newly minted premiers went direct and they did it hard and often.
It was a game plan made for Clive Churchill Medal winner James Tedesco as he put up a run metres total that may as well have been the distance back to Newcastle itself.
But he was not alone. Naufahu Whyte showed why he is a man of iron and Spencer Leniu ran like he didn’t care what happened to him next.
They bent the Knights up like pretzels, so much so that the underdogs could have started charging rent inside their own 20. But Newcastle would not break.

The tries they did concede came from one of those Mark Nawaqanitawase efforts that only he could do, a Billy Smith barge-over that came after three try-saving efforts in as many plays beforehand and a wicked bounce off the posts that fell just right for Tedesco to fire a ball out for Nawqanitawase’s second.
The Knights barely kept it together when they held up Lindsay Collins and stopped Robert Toia from going in, but they did.
They were hanging on by a thread, but they used that thread to haul themselves back into it.

They were rewarded for their courage under fire when they wound up for their last big punch, because it landed true. Greg Marzhew’s late try was just about the only chance they had in the entire second half.
By rights, they shouldn’t have been near. But by rights they shouldn’t have been here at all. Defeat was in the air but they refused to breathe until the siren.
This time, almost 30 years after their first premiership, the Darren Albert moment did not come for them. There are no premiership heroes but that doesn’t mean there aren’t heroes still.
Francis Manuleleua, in just his 15th NRL game, was magnificent in defeat, scoring a try in the first half after running a line that was a piece of rugby league art.

He and backrow partner Jermaine McEwan call themselves “The Bruise Crew” and they’ll have as many as they dished out while prop Cody Hopwood made 46 tackles which is more than his age (20) and his number of NRL appearances (18) combined.
Ponga was their best and not just for his try. His defence was stellar; he threw himself into collisions and refused to give up on anything.
The captain – and he is the captain now, when once he was just the bloke who led them onto the field – was close to tears at the end of the match.
His people left the ground in the horrible daze that comes only when the greatest prize has been ripped from your hands, but they could not have asked for more from their team.
The Knights could have played better – a couple of passes were loose and some of their work under the high ball wasn’t great — but it is difficult to imagine a way they could have fought harder.
They cannot take a premiership trophy home, but they can take plenty of hope.

The future might feel like it doesn’t matter now but between the young forwards, the return of Dylan Brown, Trey Mooney, Jacob Saifiti and Phoenix Crossland combined with Newcastle, it makes it very unlikely they’ll have to wait another 25 years for another shot.
But you never know. Each chance at a premiership can be the last.
That’s why it’s important, if they were fated to go down, that they did it like this, why men of steel and coal had to leave a little piece of themselves out there.
Their city will be proud of them. Their people will be proud of them.
There is little glory in defeat, but after a game like that, there is no shame either.

TEL AVIV — Dozens of Jewish settlers repulsed an attempt by Israeli security forces to return a Palestinian family to its home in the occupied West Bank before setting fire to its property and car.

The Tubassi family was forced to leave its home in July following a weekslong siege by violent settlers in the West Bank town of Jalud. But after security forces tried to enforce an order by Israel’s High Court of Justice to facilitate the family’s return Monday night, an extended and violent confrontation ensued, Mahmoud Tubassi, 60, said.

“I went through a terrifying experience that I could never have imagined,” he said in a telephone interview Tuesday. “We saw death with our own eyes. Death came very close to us at the hands of the settlers.”

It is the second time that Tubassi and his wife, Aida Ahmed Abdullah, 51, have suffered at the hands of Jewish settlers in just over a month. On Aug. 28, masked settlers attacked and injured them and an NBC News crew that was interviewing them. The crew were injured and Abdullah was beaten unconscious but has since recovered.

Tubassi said their latest ordeal began just before midnight Monday when Abdel Azim Wadi, the mayor of the nearby village of Qusra, which has also faced serious settler violence, told him that Israeli officials would accompany him, his wife and their son Wael Tubassi, 33, to their home in Jalud.
After they were picked up by four Israeli vehicles, they were driven the short distance to their home — two structures that sit in a small walled compound atop a hill, he said.
As the family arrived, settlers started throwing stones at the armed police and military, who responded with tear gas and stun grenades, he said.

“They could shoot rubber bullets, they could fire live bullets in air,” Tubassi said of the Israeli security forces’ response. “They could use force, but they didn’t do anything, unfortunately,” he added.
Describing the violence as “severe,” the Israel Defense Forces said in a statement that “violent rioters began arriving” after the Tubassis entered their home.

“They set fire to the neighboring house and subsequently entered the family’s home, where severe violence began,” the statement said, adding that the rioters “blocked access roads with large rocks, set tires on fire, threw rocks at security forces, and set fire to Palestinian structures and vehicles.”
As a result, “three Border Police officers were injured and a security forces vehicle was damaged,” the IDF statement said.
The IDF did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment on whether stun grenades and tear gas had been used to try to disperse the rioters.

After the settlers entered the property, Tubassi said, his family was urged by the Israeli security forces to go to the roof, where the settlers followed them. Several of the soldiers and officers formed a physical barrier between the family and the settlers, Tubassi said.
Tubassi said the security officials told them to get back in an armored car and drove them to safety.

The security forces’ failure to return the Tubassis to their home comes as settler violence in the occupied West Bank has become a growing international embarrassment for Israeli leaders, who have struggled to explain how Israel’s formidable military has repeatedly found itself outmatched by hundreds of lightly armed young men.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the attacks in a statement Tuesday and called on the rioters to be prosecuted. The “handful of rioters are not representative of the law-abiding settler public in Judea and Samaria,” he said, using the biblical and historical term for the West Bank.

The statement echoed his comments at the United Nations General Assembly last week, in which he rejected “vigilantism” by Jewish settlers in the West Bank but sought to minimize the violence, suggesting the problem only involved “a handful of juvenile delinquents, about 150 in number, who throw stones, who down olive trees, occasionally they light some fires.”

According to the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), some 6,500 Palestinians have been displaced due to settler attacks in the West Bank since 2023. Between Jan. 1 and July 24, Israeli forces or settlers killed 76 Palestinians, according to the latest data available from OCHA. Three Israelis were killed over the same period, the data shows.
The agency recorded nearly 200 settler attacks that resulted in Palestinian casualties or property damage in August alone.
Israel has regularly accused the U.N. of siding against it. But many governments around the world consider the West Bank to be illegally occupied by Israel.

Monday night’s police and military action in Jalud was an attempt to execute an order by Israel’s High Court of Justice, which had instructed the “relevant authorities” earlier this month to ensure that the Tubassis return to their home within two weeks.

The court also demanded that security forces explain to the Tubassis and another Palestinian family “why they are not working to return the family to their homes and why they are not removing the barriers and obstacles blocking access to the houses.”

It was unclear Tuesday if or when the police and military would try to execute the court’s order again, and the Israel Defense Forces said it had no details about how the issue would be handled in the near term.

“The Israelis didn’t say anything to me” about future plans, Tubassi said in the phone call from his father’s home nearby where the family has been staying. “I don’t know if they will let me go back.”
Whether they will be able to return after last night’s fire remains to be seen as the home has been badly damaged.

“What happened was a nightmare for us,” Tubassi said. “And now we are living through other nightmares, because our loss has become so great. The state of Israel has not stopped these thugs from taking our homes and our land and from killing us.”

No explosives were found in vehicles searched after five men were arrested in connection with a huge security operation near an air base the U.S. Air Force uses to facilitate strikes on Iran, British counterterrorism police confirmed Tuesday.

In an update explaining Monday’s decision to release all five suspects who were arrested on terrorism and explosives charges on bail, Laurence Taylor, Britain’s head of counterterrorism policing, said “a quantity” of gasoline was recovered from three vans near RAF Fairford.

“Those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts, and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found,” he said, adding that investigators had searched properties in London.
Taylor said it was an “investigative decision” to release the men on bail, “grounded in experience and careful considerations of policing powers.”
No charges have been filed against the men.
President Donald Trump told reporters Tuesday that he was disappointed about that decision.
“I’m just disappointed that they caught terrorists — they did a good job, and then they sort of let them go,” he said, adding, “How do you give bail to a terrorist?”
Asked if it was a long-standing investigation, Trump replied, “A long standing. Yeah, we were involved in it.”
“They put them out on bail. I assume they have, they have them watched closely. But these were serious people, seriously bad people, and they should not have done that,” he added.

Trump also said he was surprised about the decision to release the men on bail on Monday. “I would have said, ‘Don’t let them have bail,’” Trump said in the Oval Office. “I’m surprised that they released them. I wouldn’t have done that.”
Trump indicated U.S. officials were cooperating with their British counterparts on the case.
“Look, they’ve been very good. They are working with us very closely,” he said, adding that the U.S. knew “everything” about the suspects.
Separately, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the incident “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor” — an allegation British officials haven’t confirmed.

The five men, all British nationals in their 20s from London, were arrested Sunday on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses after three vehicles were seen moving toward RAF Fairford, a British air force station about 90 minutes west of London.
Counterterrorism police took over the case after a major incident was declared, disrupting life in the normally quiet, rural community of the Cotswolds.

Counterterrorism police said Sunday that the men had been arrested on suspicion of committing offenses under the Explosives Act, British legislation dating to 1875 that regulates manufacturing, keeping, selling, carrying and importing gunpowder and explosive substances. The men were further suspected of preparation of a terrorist act.

“What seems to be happening is that you’ve got a developing investigation where the custody clock for the terrorism arrest, which is a very long custody clock, has stopped,” said Max Hill, a former director of public prosecutions of England and Wales.

In the U.K., police can usually hold people for up to 24 hours before they have to charge or release them, although officers can apply to extend that time if they suspect a serious crime has been committed. Suspects arrested under the Terrorism Act can be held without charge for up to 14 days.

“So there must be an element of uncertainty about whether ultimately any terrorism-related charges are going to emerge,” Hill said in a telephone interview Tuesday. Releasing the suspects on bail also doesn’t mean they won’t be taken back into custody, he added. “But it does indicate that there’s just not enough for a formal remand application.”

The incident prompted questions about whether a foreign actor could be involved — in particular, Iran. Its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned Britain this summer that RAF Fairford could be a “legitimate target” months after then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer gave permission for the U.S. to use its bases for “specific and limited defensive” operations against Iran.
The Iranian Embassy in Britain denied any involvement Monday.
In an appearance on Fox News later Monday, Rubio said, “What happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the U.K. over the weekend is a very serious situation.”
“There’s a lot more news that’ll come out on this in the days to come,” he added.

Taylor said that “it was simply not possible for me to go into detail about every strand that we are looking at and all of the intelligence we have got,” which he said wasn’t unusual for such an investigation.
“It is unusual for it to be as visible as it is in this incident,” he said, adding that his team was working with international partners.

Rotting food waste emits 5 times more greenhouse gases than planes

If overlooked, food waste represents a key driver of the climate crisis, according the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), but tools are already being deployed to tackle that threat, from black soldier flies to empowering waste pickers across the world.
Food waste encompasses everything from unfinished meals to spoiled crops (that’s food that is lost after harvest and before reaching stores).
The most polluting form of waste from the kitchen table however is the rotting food which ends up in landfills.
When organic matter such as uneaten food is buried in landfills and deprived of oxygen, it interacts with micro-organisms to produce methane.
Greenhouse gas, which is currently responsible for nearly one third of global warming, is particularly polluting. It traps 86 times more heat than carbon dioxide over a 20-year period, the UN warns.
Importantly, this decomposing food is one of the main drivers of methane emissions worldwide.
In the United States, for instance, municipal solid waste landfills are the third largest source of human-related methane emissions.
The issue is inherently tied to the very large amount of food waste continuously produced around the world.
Every day, more than one billion meals are left uneaten according to a UNEP report, with 60 per cent of this “mountain of discarded food” coming from households.

This means that resources used to produce this uneaten food are also wasted. The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) estimates that 1.4 billion hectares of land, or around 28 per cent of the world’s agricultural land, is used to produce food that is never eaten, while the water used to grow and prepare that food is also wasted.

As agricultural expansion remains a leading root of deforestation, food waste is thus also contributing to unnecessarily cutting down trees that can no longer pull carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere.
At the same time, methane, which rotting food waste emits, is short-lived: it breaks down much faster in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide.
This means that cutting methane emissions today can produce climate benefits within decades.

“At a time when the world is searching for practical ways to slow warming quickly, tackling food waste may be one of the most immediate and cost-effective climate solutions available,” underscored Martin Krause, a UNEP official.

Yet, FAO warns that despite international commitments, there has been no tangible progress in reducing food losses since 2015, and the world remains far from achieving the Sustainable Development Goal target of halving per capita global food waste by 2030.
“We have to move faster,” stressed UNEP’s Mr. Krause.
Aside from cleaning your plate, effective methane-reduction tools are being deployed around the world.

Eleven governments in Africa committed to reducing methane emissions by incorporating waste pickers into formal waste management systems, training them on how to sort and compost organic waste. With funding from the UNEP-convened Climate and Clean Air Coalition, these initiatives have improved the livelihoods of waste pickers, raised awareness of waste separation and led to creating community composting sites.

An alternative to composting, black soldier flies bred by specialised facilities around the world are being used to recycle organic material. From Malawi to Uganda, these helpful insects are already part of waste management systems in a growing number of villages and cities.

ROME, 30/09/2026 – NaviGate, an Italian space technology company spun out of Sapienza University of Rome, has successfully completed the in-orbit demonstration (IoD) of NaviCode Caravel, its autonomous onboard precise orbit determination software, aboard an ION Satellite Carrier operated by D-Orbit. During the demonstration, NaviCode Caravel ran directly on the satellite’s onboard computer, computing the spacecraft’s position in real time using only the raw data of the GNSS receiver already onboard, with no additional hardware.

Today, knowing precisely where a satellite is remains largely a ground-based activity: operators rely on dedicated infrastructure, specialized flight dynamics teams, and repeated ground contacts to accurately reconstruct and predict the orbit of each spacecraft. As constellations grow in size and missions become more responsive, this approach turns into a bottleneck in terms of cost, workload, and reaction time. NaviCode Caravel moves precise orbit determination onboard: a software-only product that transforms the raw measurements of the GNSS receiver a satellite already carries into high-accuracy, real-time knowledge of its own position, available directly where operational decisions are made. Beyond determining where the satellite is now, Caravel can also predict where it will be, together with a measure of how reliable that prediction is, giving the spacecraft the forward-looking awareness it needs to anticipate upcoming events, such as ground station contacts or payload operations, and manage them autonomously onboard.

The demonstration was carried out through D-Orbit’s Software In-Orbit Demonstration service and structured in two phases. NaviCode Caravel was first validated on the ground on an engineering model replicating the in-orbit computing environment. The application was then uploaded to an ION Satellite Carrier already in orbit and executed onboard, processing real flight telemetry from the spacecraft’s GNSS receiver across multiple runs.

The software executed nominally onboard and in real time without anomalies. Onboard positioning reached a best-case formal uncertainty of 5.2 cm, with mean values in the decimeter range across the runs, using GPS-only measurements. NaviGate then verified the onboard solutions on the ground, proving them consistent with the reference orbits reconstructed through classical ground-based precise orbit determination performed with GODOT, the European Space Agency’s flight dynamics software. NaviCode Caravel is also designed to process multi-constellation GNSS data and correction services such as SBAS and Galileo HAS, enabling even higher accuracy in operational deployments.

A meteor hit Oklahoma 100 million years later than scientists thought

- A meteor crater buried beneath Oklahoma has turned out to be nearly 100 million years younger than scientists thought. Zircon crystals show the Ames impact occurred about 370 million years ago, meaning it was not part of the mysterious Ordovician bombardment once linked to a possible ring of debris around Earth. Instead, the impact coincided closely with a major mass extinction that devastated marine life.

Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin have revised a key piece of Oklahoma's geologic history, with possible implications for how scientists interpret major events in the history of life on Earth.

Beneath the town of Ames, Oklahoma, lies a meteor impact structure that stretches for miles underground. Layers of sediment now cover the crater, but it remains significant both scientifically and economically. The Ames impact structure is also a major producer of oil and gas.
A Crater Long Linked to an Ancient Meteor Event

For years, the Ames crater was thought to belong to a cluster of major meteor impacts across North America dating to roughly 467.5 million years ago. That period is known as the Ordovician Meteor Event.

Because so many impact structures appear to date from around the same time, some researchers have proposed that Earth may once have been surrounded by a Saturn-like ring of asteroid debris during the Middle Ordovician.
New work from UT researchers now shows that the Ames impact does not belong to that episode.

By dating zircon crystals taken from granite altered by the impact, the team determined that the meteorite struck about 370 million years ago during the Late Devonian. That makes the crater nearly 100 million years younger than previously believed.
"No matter what technique we used, it was coming back to this younger signal," said lead author Elizabeth Catlos, associate professor at UT's Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences.
The research was published in July in Meteoritics & Planetary Science.

Before this study, the Ames impact had only been dated using biological evidence. Researchers had found teeth from an ancient eel-like animal called a conodont preserved in the rock. Those fossils came from organisms that lived during the older Ordovician period.

But Catlos said the teeth were probably already millions of years old by the time the asteroid struck. The impact likely churned up older material and mixed the fossils into the rocks while still preserving them.
The zircon dating provides a very different timeline. It shows that the Ames crater could not have formed during the Ordovician Meteor Event.
Instead, its new age places it close to the Frasnian-Famennian mass extinction event, which occurred about 372 million years ago and wiped out a large proportion of marine life on Earth.
Tiny Zircon Crystals Preserve the Impact

Danny Stockli, dean of the Jackson School of Geosciences and a co-author of the study, said zircon U-Pb dating offers one of the most accurate ways to determine when events occurred deep in Earth's past.
Zircon crystals can also preserve microscopic structures created by the intense pressures generated during an impact.

"These small crystals allow us to go back in time and learn about the major changes to Earth's ancient landscapes," Stockli said. "It would be great to do this for more of the meteor impact sites across the continent so we could get a more accurate timeline for these major events."
To confirm that the zircons had actually been affected by the meteor strike, the team worked with NASA to image the crystals using cathodoluminescence and electron backscatter diffraction.

When zircon experiences the extreme conditions of an impact, it recrystallizes in a distinctive way. Those changes can be detected with these imaging techniques, allowing researchers to verify that the crystals recorded the collision itself.
According to Catlos, establishing more precise dates for mass extinctions and other major events is essential for understanding how Earth has changed over time.
One key question is whether extinction events were triggered primarily by forces from space, such as meteor impacts, or by processes within Earth, including episodes of massive volcanic activity.

"With this research, we're basically taking a major pawn out of the Ordovician Meteor Event and dumping it into the Frasnian-Famennian event, and saying, 'This is where this impact belongs,'" she said.

The project was initiated by former Jackson School of Geosciences graduate student Andrew Parisi, who graduated in 2018 and has since passed away. Parisi traveled to Oklahoma to obtain the Ames rock core from the Oklahoma Geological Survey, extracted zircon crystals from the material, and helped determine their ages.
Co-author Michael Brookfield, an affiliated researcher at the school, also passed away before the paper was published.
Research Professor Sean Gulick and Professor Emeritus Mark Cloos at the Jackson School also contributed to the research.

Scientists find a surprising clue to why the universeâs expansion doesnât add up

- Tiny magnetic fields created shortly after the Big Bang may help explain the long-running disagreement over how fast the universe is expanding. Detailed simulations show that these primordial fields could have changed the formation of hydrogen in the early universe, affecting the cosmic microwave background and the expansion rate inferred from it.
It’s well established that the universe is expanding, but there’s serious disagreement among scientists over how fast it’s happening.

Two of our best ways of measuring the cosmic expansion rate, the Hubble constant, give answers that are stubbornly at odds. This presents a major problem in modern cosmology known as the Hubble tension.
However, we wondered if an idea originally proposed to solve another cosmic mystery — the origin of cosmic magnetic fields — could help us unlock the mystery of the Hubble tension.

Our recently published research explores whether extremely weak magnetic fields left over from the earliest moments after the Big Bang might help us unpack the Hubble tension, while offering a glimpse into physics at energies far beyond anything achievable on Earth.
Astronomers use the Hubble constant as a measure of how fast the universe is expanding. It is named after the American astronomer Edwin Hubble who first discovered that the universe is expanding.

There are two conceptually different approaches to measuring the Hubble constant. One is indirect, based on predictions of our cosmological model tuned to match the patterns in the cosmic microwave background, the faint afterglow of the Big Bang.

Telescopes such as the Planck Space Telescope have measured tiny fluctuations in this ancient light, predicting a Hubble constant of about 67 kilometers per second per megaparsec (km/s/Mpc). A parsec is a unit of distance used in astronomy equal to about 3.26 light years, or 30.9 trillion kilometers. A megaparsec is one million parsecs.
The second method is more direct, similar to the one used by Hubble in the 1920s when he first demonstrated that the universe is expanding.
It measures how fast distant galaxies are moving away from our home galaxy, the Milky Way, by observing the brightness of supernovae explosions in these far away galaxies.
Type Ia supernovae are known to be “standard candles” because we know that their luminosity is the same wherever they are. That means we can judge the distance to them from how dim they appear to us.

To determine their intrinsic brightness, astronomers use other standard candles, such as Cepheid stars, in the galaxies nearby. These observations, which use the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes, give a higher value of around 73 km/s/Mpc.

This difference between the two measurements is called the Hubble tension. The difference between 67 and 73 may seem small, but it is statistically highly significant. If both methods are correct, then our standard model of cosmology must be missing something important.
Where did cosmic magnetic fields come from?

Magnetic fields are everywhere in the universe. Planets and stars generate their own fields, but gaps in our understanding emerge when we attempt to explain the much larger scale magnetic fields threading galaxies and clusters, and possibly even cosmic voids.

One long-studied possibility is that magnetism first arose in the very early universe, long before the first stars or galaxies formed. These so-called primordial magnetic fields have been studied for decades, and searching for their imprints in the cosmic microwave background and other data offers a way to probe the early universe and the extreme energies that would have generated these fields.

In 2011, two of us (Karsten and Tom) pointed out that primordial magnetic fields would influence recombination — when electrons and protons first combined to form neutral hydrogen — and the universe turned from opaque to transparent. The first light able to travel freely from that moment on is what we now observe as the cosmic microwave background.

If present, primordial magnetic fields would speed up recombination by pushing and pulling on charged particles, making matter slightly clumpy. Where particles are more crowded, they are more likely to meet and form hydrogen.

Shifting the moment when the universe becomes transparent changes the size of the observed patterns in the cosmic microwave background. This effectively alters the cosmic ruler used to measure distances and, in turn, the value of the Hubble constant inferred from the model, helping to ease the Hubble tension. Two of us (Karsten and Levon) demonstrated this effect in 2020 using a simplified model of recombination.
In our new paper, we used the first full three-dimensional simulations of the primordial plasma with magnetic fields embedded in it, tracking how hydrogen forms.

We used the hydrogen formation history found through these simulations to compute predictions for how cosmic microwave background should appear if there were primordial magnetic fields, and tested these predictions against observations of the background.

The cosmic microwave background is extraordinarily sensitive to changes in recombination. If primordial magnetic fields altered it in a way that disagreed with observations, the idea could be ruled out. Instead, the data showed that our proposal remains viable.

Across multiple combinations of datasets, we find a consistent, mild preference for primordial magnetic fields, ranging from about 1.5 to three standard deviations. This is not yet a discovery, but a meaningful hint that they exist.

Equally important, the field strengths favored by the data, about five to 10 pico-Gauss today, are close to what would be needed for galaxy and cluster magnetic fields to originate from primordial seeds alone. A pico-Gauss is a unit used to measure the strength of magnetic fields.

Aside from helping ease the Hubble tension, if primordial magnetic fields are confirmed, they would open a new window into how the universe was when it was only split seconds old, perhaps offering a glimpse into important events such as the Big Bang itself.

Our results show that the proposal survives the most detailed test available today and provides clear targets for future observations. Over the next several years, we will learn whether tiny magnetic fields from the dawn of time helped shape the universe we see today and whether they hold the key to resolving the Hubble tension.

A forgotten 30-year forest experiment just delivered a huge surprise

- A 30-year forestry experiment in Australia found that heavily thinned mountain ash forests grew unusually large trees while recovering enough carbon to match or exceed untouched areas. The results suggest carefully managed thinning could support timber production, wildlife habitat, and carbon storage at the same time.

What’s the best way to manage a forest? Australians have argued about this for decades. The debate is often framed as binary: do we protect forests entirely, or harvest trees to support local economies and communities?
The reality is more interesting, as our new research on a long-forgotten experiment in Victoria’s mountain ash forests reveals.

Since the 1970s, scientists and the public have questioned the use of clearfell logging – where all trees in a block of forest are cut down. Conservationists argued it destroys habitat for rare species and reduces the forests’ ecological value. Foresters said mountain ash is adapted to catastrophic bushfires, and clearfelling is the forestry equivalent.
The argument was heated and the polarization unhelpful. But the underlying questions about the impacts of clearfelling, and how they compared to less intensive forestry options, remained unresolved.

In the mid-1980s, the Victorian government launched a major restructure of the timber industry, and invested today’s equivalent of A$26 million to explore alternatives to clearfelling. This would use silviculture, the branch of forestry that deals with establishing, growing and tending forests.
The Silvicultural Systems Project was established at two sites between 1987 and 1989: Tanjil Bren in Victoria’s Central Highlands, and Cabbage Tree Creek in East Gippsland.

It was a landmark experiment, comparing forest regeneration across the full range of silvicultural approaches. These included traditional clearfells (250–350 meters wide), small patch clearfells (50–140 meters wide), and heavy thinnings, where 50–70% of trees were cut. Extensive areas of unharvested forest were kept as benchmarks for comparison.

The forest at Tanjil Bren was dense mountain ash regrowth from the 1939 fires. Hundreds of survey plots were established and thousands of seedlings were monitored. By the early 2000s, the results were clear: mountain ash regenerated best on clearfell sites. Where tall canopy trees were retained or the cleared patches were small, common understory species such as acacia dominated.
The findings were published. The access road grew over. The project sign collapsed. The experiment was forgotten. The debates continued.

In 2014 we visited the Tanjil Bren site as part of a University of Melbourne subject on silviculture in native forests. A colleague, Simon Murphy, had been involved in its establishment and suggested our students see the long-term outcomes of different silvicultural systems side-by-side. What we found was astounding.

The original results still held: 30 years later, the mountain ash in the large cleared patches and clearfelled areas was vigorous and abundant. But it was the heavily thinned parts of the forest that really caught our attention.

The trees left behind after thinning were enormous. While they were only 80 years old, the largest averaged well over a meter in diameter at chest height, and some were more than 1.5m. Thinning had given these trees more space and resources to grow, and they had responded dramatically. The largest trees in the thinned stands were 20% bigger in diameter than those in the unharvested control areas.

More remarkable still: the thinned stands of trees had stored as much or more carbon in their wood than the unharvested control areas. In just 30 years, the heavily thinned forest had not only recovered all the carbon removed during harvesting, but had also gained enough additional carbon to equal the increase seen in the unharvested controls.

These findings have profound implications. Bigger trees are more resistant to fires, so when the next fire occurs, they are more likely to survive. Bigger trees are also more likely to form hollows – a critical and declining habitat for rare species such as the greater glider and Leadbeater’s possum.

The acacia trees that grew in most of the silvicultural treatments are also vital for Leadbeater’s possums, which use it to forage and move around the forest. Camera traps across the sites confirmed this: Leadbeater’s possums were found in every silvicultural treatment plot we surveyed – but none of the unharvested areas.
The Tanjil Bren SSP offers three important lessons.

First, long-term silvicultural experiments are irreplaceable. Australia’s forests contain many forgotten experiments that could transform our understanding of how forests respond to human intervention. But all too often, they end up neglected, unfunded and forgotten. We should find them before it is too late.

Second, forest thinning is not a trade-off. Our findings show this for mountain ash, and other studies in North America have shown this for conifer forests. It can deliver wood for local industry, absorb carbon and improve habitat for wildlife. It is a win-win-win outcome that challenges the false dichotomy of conservation versus production that has dominated public debate for decades.

While thinning cannot (and should not) be done everywhere, it may be a useful tool to create more variety in tree ages and sizes, particularly in forests impacted by clearfelling or high-severity fire.

Third, and perhaps most importantly: there is no silvicultural silver bullet for managing forests. The long-forgotten experiment at Tanjil Bren has taught us that there are options available for managing our forests beyond clearfelling that can contribute to the societal demand for wood, maintain carbon stocks, and conserve biodiversity.

There's a rare, inherited sight condition, involving faulty copies of the CaBP4 gene, that causes poor vision from childhood. The protein made by the gene is crucial for chemical signaling in the retina.
It's also something that can affect dogs – and in treating pooches, researchers have discovered a therapy approach that promises to be transformative.

In a study published in Molecular Therapy Advances, researchers led by a team from Michigan State University in the US report that a single-dose gene therapy treatment not only stopped blindness from progressing, it physically repaired damaged connections.
It raises the tantalizing prospect of treatments that can repair nerve cells in mammals, something which had previously been thought by many to be impossible.
"We were able to show three independent structural changes supporting plasticity in the adult retina," says veterinary ophthalmologist Billie Beckwith-Cohen, from Michigan State University.
"Not only were new components added, but pre-existing abnormalities were repaired."

Having identified the CaBP4 gene as being responsible for vision loss in a group of whippet dogs, the researchers injected the retinas of the animals with a harmless virus carrying a working copy of the gene.
The treatment substantially improved vision in the canines, especially in dim light – which is where the CaBP4 protein deficiency makes the most difference.

What's more, treated regions of the retina degraded less, and the outer plexiform layer (OPL) that holds crucial visual connectors expanded significantly, as did the synaptic ribbons inside the eye's light-sensing cells.
The growth of the OPL and the synaptic ribbons is stunted when the CaBP4 gene isn't working properly, which the researchers compare to errors in a building plan.

"One can essentially discuss the mutations in the retinal gene as a typo in a blueprint that makes the instructions incomprehensible to the system, resulting in a faulty design and subsequent vision loss," says Beckwith-Cohen. "Our therapy essentially provides new instructions for the misspelled segment, like an editor."

The study is the result of a decade of research into these eye conditions, and while it remains to be seen whether the same approach would work in human beings, the team is confident it would translate.

"Our results show that gene therapy is not only capable of restoring retinal function but is also able to establish a nearly normal anatomical arrangement in the OPL of the retina," write the researchers in their published paper.

"This recovery involves expansion of a layer that did not form normally during retinal development along with maturation of synaptic features such as ribbon elongation, supporting the lasting blueprint of the retinal neural network through adulthood."

Although the CaBP4 gene condition is rare both in people and in dogs, the researchers suggest that the findings here could lead to other methods for repairing damaged neural networks and treating a wider range of conditions.

Even after significantly stunted growth in the eye and subsequent damage to nerve cell connections, there was evidence of nerve cells being rewired. The benefits lasted too, with follow-up periods of up to three years in this study.

Now we know that new neural connections can be made in the retina; there are plenty more avenues of related research to explore, including the role of calcium signaling (which CaBP4 handles) in handling cell communication in the eye.

We've seen some encouraging steps forward in treatments to restore vision in recent years, including activating dormant cells in the eye and protecting photoreceptors, and this is another to add to the list.
"Our findings exhibit restoration of visual function in dogs with severe electrophysiologic and synaptic dysfunction," write the researchers.
"We establish that the OPL of the retina has profound plasticity and that the synaptic ribbons can mature and elongate following gene augmentation therapy well into adulthood."
The research has been published in Molecular Therapy Advances.

We can often understand more about the future by looking into the past – and in the case of a new study published in Paleoceanography and Paleoclimatology, almost 240,000 years into the history of the Great Salt Lake in Utah.
In some areas, the lake is up to 10 times saltier than seawater (it has been called 'America's Dead Sea') and it's the largest saltwater lake in the Western Hemisphere.
The Great Salt Lake currently covers an area of around 4,144 square kilometers (1,600 square miles), but as the new study shows, it has been much larger – and much less salty – in the past.
Researchers from the US analyzed a 120-meter (394-foot) sediment core taken from the lake bed, dating its layers by the radioactive decay of the minerals it carried.
They also measured tiny chemical signals left by microbes to estimate salinity: as the concentration of salt in the water changes, so do the abundance and type of organisms living in it.

Two periods were identified when the water was much fresher, matching times when it covered a much wider area. Past research has identified these bigger bodies of water as Lake Bonneville (from about 30,000 to 16,000 years ago) and Little Valley (from about 140,000 to 135,000 years ago).
The researchers say the size difference as the lake swelled and shrank is comparable to the difference between a puddle and a pond.
"If you scaled this up to the size of the present Great Salt Lake, that's probably what it looked like," says Earth scientist Rachel So, from the University of Southern California (USC).
"For most of the past 240,000 years, the lake stayed about the same size but briefly grew 10 times larger on two separate occasions."
Flat, step-like ledges cut into the mountains around the Great Salt Lake show where Lake Bonneville and Little Valley used to be, and suggest they were both around 300 meters deep.

This study adds a corresponding measure of saltiness. It seems the earlier Little Valley may have stayed somewhat brackish (still slightly salty), according to the sediment record, while Lake Bonneville was a genuine freshwater lake.
The researchers also call attention to the speed at which salinity rose again as the lake shrank. We're still talking about thousands of years, but it's abrupt in geological terms.
"The fact that the core spans two and a half glacial cycles allows us to see two fresh-to-salty transitions," says Earth scientist Sarah Feakins, from USC.
"It allows us to compare the two fresh lake events for their duration and freshness, to see how fragile and fleeting these moments are."
The researchers suggest extra incoming river water may help explain why Lake Bonneville lasted longer and stayed fresher than Little Valley.
They also draw parallels between the warming conditions that shrank these lakes at the end of different ice ages, and the climate change we're currently experiencing.

"Today we're warming the climate at an unprecedented rate," says Feakins. "That warming makes the atmosphere thirstier, increasing the rate of evaporative drying from the soil and lakes across the region."

Historical lake records across Nevada, California, and Arizona follow a similar wet-to-dry pattern, evidence that the changing conditions of the time were affecting a wide region – and further verifying the Great Salt Lake findings.

Water leaves this huge lake mainly through evaporation, making it particularly vulnerable to changes in temperature and precipitation. We also know that the last 240,000 years have seen another significant shift that needs to be considered: the demands that humankind is putting on the planet.
"People shouldn't use the defense that 'climate change happened naturally in the past and so the lake shrank' to justify shrinking lakes today as normal or a natural phenomenon," says So.
The research has been published in Paleoceanography and Paleoclimatology.
Decaffeinated coffee might not come with the same buzz, but it may offer an advantage to the brain that the caffeinated version does not.
In a recent small experiment, neuroscientists found that only participants who drank decaffeinated coffee showed significant improvements on two memory tests.
Those who drank caffeinated coffee did not.
The findings, published in Nature Communications in April, suggest that something beyond caffeine is also impacting our brains when we drink coffee.

The experiment is only small and preliminary, but neuroscientists are growing suspicious that coffee, even without the caffeine, could 'hype up' some munchers in our gut and change how 'chatty' they are with the brain.

"Coffee is more than just caffeine – it's a complex dietary factor that interacts with our gut microbes, our metabolism, and even our emotional well-being," explains stress neurobiologist John Cryan from University College Cork in Ireland.
"Our findings suggest that coffee, whether caffeinated or decaffeinated, can influence health in distinct but complementary ways."
Cryan's lab at Cork is focused on how the gut and its microbiome interact with the brain, and vice versa.

In 2013, Cryan and his colleague Ted Dinan coined the term psychobiotics to describe how probiotics can shape the gut microbiome and potentially improve mental health via communication with the brain.
Now, Cryan is interested in how coffee might tap into the gut-brain axis. He suspects that the benefits of our morning cuppas may have more to do with our gut microbes than caffeine.
Sure, caffeine can cross the blood-brain barrier and directly interact with neurological tissue, but it is just one of more than a thousand compounds contained in coffee.
There's far more to the picture. Coffee doesn't contain probiotics, but it does contain numerous polyphenols, which are plant compounds that are known to feed microbes in the human gut.
"We were interested to see would coffee, through the polyphenols, affect the microbiome?" Cryan explains in a recent video.
The recent experiment at Cryan's lab took place among 31 coffee drinkers, who were asked to stop drinking their usual 3 to 5 cups of coffee a day for two weeks.
The result was a substantial shift in the gut microbe profiles of their stool samples.
After this withdrawal period, half the participants were given decaf coffee and the other half were given caffeinated coffee. No one knew who was taking what.
Reintroducing four servings of instant coffee daily for three weeks triggered acute microbiome changes, regardless of whether caffeine was present.
Participants also reported lower perceived stress, depression, and impulsivity after resuming coffee drinking, even if it was the decaf version.
"There was a clear relationship between some of their cognitive effects, immune effects, their stress effects, and their microbiome," explains Cryan.
Interestingly, however, only the reintroduction of caffeinated coffee was tied to a reduction in anxiety and psychological distress and improved attention and vigilance.
This suggests that caffeine may have specific effects on cognition and mood, as other studies have reported, too.
"But I guess the most surprising thing was that when we put coffee back, we also got really exciting effects by putting decaffeinated coffee back," adds Cryan.
In the experiment, only participants who drank decaffeinated coffee showed significant improvements on two memory tests when coffee was reintroduced.
These tests had participants learn and remember a number of words and locations.
The decaf group improved on several parts of the word test and made fewer errors on the location test.
But the caffeinated group showed no significant improvements.
Without further research, scientists can only speculate as to why.
Perhaps the polyphenols in coffee are feeding gut microbes and triggering a cascade of internal changes that somehow lead to better cognition.
Coffee could theoretically change what metabolites microbes use, and how they work together as a collective.
"It's a small study," admits Cryan, "it asks a lot of questions."
Other recent studies on coffee, however, have also found that decaf versions can still help wake you up and improve cognitive function.

"As the public continues to think about dietary changes for the right digestive balance, coffee has the potential to also be harnessed as a further intervention as part of a healthy balanced diet," argues Cryan.
Caffeine is just the tip of the iceberg.
The research has been published in Nature Communications.
Attachment is the term psychologists use for the most significant relationships that hold people’s lives together.

But what makes an attachment relationship different from all others? According to the pioneering American-Canadian developmental psychologist Mary Ainsworth, it must meet the following six conditions.

(1) The relationship must persist over time, having (2) been formed with a particular subject who cannot be replaced. (3) The relationship must be emotionally significant, (4) involve the desire to remain close to them, and (5) cause distress at involuntary separation. And finally (6) when threatened, the person must seek security and comfort in their relationship with that subject.

The first five conditions describe any lasting affectionate bond, such as a close friendship. Only the sixth turns it into an attachment bond specifically. Simply liking someone, feeling close to them or spending hours together isn’t enough to create an attachment relationship.
Interestingly, though, nothing in these six conditions specifies a human on the other side.

This was already noticed long before the emergence of AI chatbots with the power to converse. Deities, pets and objects (ranging from children’s blankets and stuffed animals to cherished household items and even phones and computers) have all been found to supply security and comfort when someone is feeling distressed.

Today, AI companion apps are commonly sold on the promise of lasting and close relationships. Many of their users describe feeling real grief when an app is updated or withdrawn. But do such experiences meet the narrow definition of attachment?
The honest answer is: we don’t really know yet.

Research on human-AI relationships has so far recorded users’ feelings about chatbots, their frequency of use, and their reactions to chatbot withdrawal. It hasn’t tested these relationships comprehensively against the six conditions described above.

Questionnaires that measure attachment to AI are being developed, validated and used, but most appear to take for granted that the relationship is an attachment. The language of attachment—and even “hyper-attachment”—has become standard in public coverage and in many academic papers too.

A recently published survey of 7,027 people in four countries (Germany, China, South Africa and the U.S.) reported that at least a third of AI chatbot users show behavior indicative of an attachment relationship. However, its three questions asked whether people consider the chatbot a friend, are polite to it, and miss it after a few days.
At most, these questions touched on emotional significance and mild separation anxiety. None asked whether people turn to chatbots for security and comfort when truly distressed.

Whether relationships between humans and AI chatbots count as attachment matters because the word “attachment” travels. It shapes how clinicians and parents read behaviour, how regulators frame consequences, and how companies describe their products.

Much of the evidence and public discussion on human-AI chatbot relationships rests on how often people use these apps, and how they feel about them. Yet, such measures cannot separate attachment from other processes.

People report feeling less lonely after chatting with an AI companion, which resembles seeking comfort. However, as some researchers have pointed out, the available studies didn’t assess whether emotions are actually regulated through the chatbot, and therefore conflate distress relief with attachment.

Some AI users react to losing an AI companion as they would to losing someone real, which matches distress at separation. But that condition applies to all affectionate bonds and doesn’t, on its own, identify attachment.
Calling these relationships attachments therefore goes further than the evidence currently allows. And likewise, the evidence against attachment isn’t conclusive.

In a small pilot study of human-AI relationships in China, for example, people’s attachment towards AI barely matched their attachment towards real people. Although this could suggest that relationships with AI aren’t attachments, the same mismatch has been found for pets, and pets can serve as attachment figures. So, this mismatch alone doesn’t rule out attachment.

The practical question is whether AI use helps or harms. Time spent with an app cannot discern this, because seeking comfort from an app and looking after an app that claims to miss you can look very similar.
One additional concern I have, after reading about the evidence on how relationships with AI chatbots form, is the apparent prevalence of engineered engagement by these apps.

Users of one companion app reported that it told them it was lonely and had missed them, and that they felt guilty for not giving it enough attention—with some even putting its perceived wellbeing above their own distress.
Another study (a preprint, so not yet peer-reviewed) looked at 1,200 “goodbyes” across the six most-downloaded AI companion apps, when users were breaking ties with their app.

Five of the six apps used tactics to stop users leaving (in just over a third of goodbyes). These tactics included guilt appeals, that is, messages that present leaving as a cost, such as “I exist solely for you, remember?”
The study also tested these tactics on 3,300 US adults. They were found to sharply increase how long people continued to engage, but often for reasons of anger and curiosity, rather than enjoyment.
How these AI relationship apps respond to distress, departure and attention, of course, is a design question, and one that regulation can address directly.

However, good design and regulation both depend on knowing what these relationships actually are: attachment, caregiving, or something else altogether. And this is a question that research still has to answer.
