The earliest days of Christianity are hazy—relatively few written records survive from this era, and religious artifacts are rare archaeological finds. Still, a newly discovered early Christian monastery, dating to just six centuries after the religion got its start, could offer clues to how the faith spread across the world.
In a new study published this week in the journal Antiquity, researchers describe how a group of historians helped discover the early medieval monastery in a stroke of good luck.

The site is situated on the island of Lismore and is believed to have been founded by Saint Mo Luóc, an early Christian saint also known as Moluag. Researchers had long suspected Mo Luóc’s monastery was there but hadn’t been able to prove it until the local Lismore Historical Society led an excavation in the area, which also holds the ruins of a 13th-century cathedral.
With the help of professional archaeologists, the historians uncovered ancient grave sites, buildings, pieces of sculpture and extensive evidence of craft workshops at the site.

Gordon Noble, the paper’s senior author and an archaeologist at the University of Aberdeen in Scotland, says that the evidence of craftworking is particularly exciting. The team found hundreds of clay molds and crucibles used for working bronze, silver and gold—a somewhat “unusual” find for a monastery, Noble says.
“It’s one of the largest metalworking assemblages we have from any site, secular or sacred, in this time period,” he says.
Overall, the size of the monastery suggests Lismore, which lies on Loch Linnhe on Scotland’s west coast, was likely more important to medieval Christian society than previously realized, he says.

Other sites are known to have played a major role. For example, the island of Iona, to the southwest of Lismore in Scotland, is known for being the “Cradle of Christianity.” But the new findings suggest Lismore was “a very significant mover and shaker” in the spread of the early religion, Noble says.
Noble and his colleagues plan to keep investigating the site, including an analysis of the monastery’s “vallum,” or outer boundary, often indicated by a wall or bank.
The entire monastery appears to have been “huge,” Noble says. “It’ll be really exciting to see what shows up in the coming years.”

Bruno Solari spent his August traveling all around Spain, starting with a week in Ibiza, continuing on to Madrid, Málaga, Marbella and Barcelona, before finally returning to Ibiza for a bachelor party.
He also managed to squeeze in a few meetings and client calls all throughout.

Solari, founder and CEO of the New York City-based PR firm SolComms, was among his company's 53 employees enjoying their inaugural "Work from Anywhere August." Other employees logged on from all over the U.S. (the Jersey Shore, the Hamptons, Florida) and the world (Berlin, Prague, London, Portugal).

"I was in Spain the entire month of August, and I would have felt like a hypocrite if I was going to be there and making my team be in-office," Solari, 33, tells CNBC Make It. "So I thought, 'OK, I'm doing this myself. I'm going to grant that flexibility to the entire agency.'"

The end-of-summer experiment felt like a worthwhile risk to the 3-year-old startup: Employee surveys of the trial indicate boosted productivity, work-life balance and happiness, while the business also saw a modest revenue boost. It also runs counter to several big companies scaling back on remote-work flexibility in a job market where employers have the upper hand.
"I think people were surprised that I went for it," Solari says.

Four weeks of fully remote work from anywhere in the world is a bold move for the millennial founder, who came up in PR agencies at the height of the hustle culture era and says he holds more "traditional" workplace values, like building company culture through in-person interactions rather than "through a screen" of fully remote work. Since its founding in 2023, SolComms has operated with a four days in-office requirement, with Fridays at home that end at 3 p.m. most weeks (and 12 p.m. during the summer).

Some 25% of full-time U.S. workers work in a hybrid arrangement, with the most common requirements being three days in the office, followed by four, according to a recent report from Owl Labs, a video-conferencing technology company, which surveyed 2,000 people in July. Most, 65%, work onsite full time, and 10% work remotely full time.

Solari says every year his company surveys its own employees about the perks and benefits they want, and every year they ask for more work-from-home days. Wary of granting another remote working day during the week, Solari thought to offer 100% flexibility within a one-month period instead.

He and his leadership team came up with the idea in January, announced it to employees in February, and spent the next six months coming up with best practices to make sure everyone was set up for remote success.

Among those guidelines: Stick to 9 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. EST working hours, keep cameras on for all meetings, dress for meetings as if you were going into the office, use Slack status updates liberally, take lunch and other breaks, and no sensitive calls or screens in public spaces.

SolComms also communicated their remote-August plans to the agency's 80-plus clients across healthcare, tech and AI, and consumer brands, says Natalie Valicenti, 30, the company's associate vice president of operations, who split her remote month across Rhode Island and Minnesota.
The SolComms benefit comes at a time when many company leaders are scaling back on employee flexibility and benefits, and during a tightening labor market where employers have the upper-hand.

In September, Uber announced plans to cut about 3,300 corporate jobs, as well as scale down its remote workforce and tighten in-office rules. Disney said it would require more employees to report to the office four days a week and later announced layoffs of about 300 employees.

The five-day return-to-office creep has been growing for several years. The share of Fortune 500 companies requiring five days in the office nearly doubled from mid-2024 to mid-2025, from 13% to 24%, according to research from Flex Index, a resource within the advisory firm Work Forward that analyzes office requirements data.
But for SolComms, the risks of loosening office requirements for a month seem to have paid off.

Twenty-one employees answered a survey following the inaugural remote month, with 76% saying they were more productive, 90% saying they maintained high work-life balance, and 100% saying they want Work from Anywhere August back next year, according to documents reviewed by Make It. Several say the experience helped them strengthen their communication and self-management skills, and a lot of people said cutting their commute times was the biggest draw.

There were also some downsides, like staffers saying they felt tied to their computers and found it hard to step away, whereas it felt more natural to take breaks for lunch, coffee or a walk if they were in the office.
Solari says he sees this "internal pressure to be available" as a common struggle with remote work.

"I think it's a matter of continuing to let employees know that we're flexible," he says. "You don't need to be chained to a desk to prove that you're doing a good job, and ultimately, it's not always the person who's the first to respond who's the power player in producing results."
Though not the goal, Solari says, the business also saw financial benefits: Revenue increased by a modest 4% revenue from July to August, and jumped 12% from August to September.
Solari is already committed to a return of the program in August 2027.
"[We're] 1,000% doing it again, without a doubt," he says.

OPEC+ agreed to keep oil production targets steady for November at a meeting on Sunday, the producer group said, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year.

Seven core members of the group comprising the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia made the decision for November in a brief online meeting on Sunday. The core members are Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman.

Gulf OPEC+ producers have been pumping well below output targets in the face of continuing export disruptions from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, with exports fluctuating at 60% to 80% of normal levels in recent months.

"The OPEC+ group of seven kept their production ceilings unchanged, in line with market expectations. That said, despite rising flows through the Strait of Hormuz, their output levels remain well below quota," said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo.
"Consequently, the oil market remains tight."

Oil prices had dropped on Friday after European leaders agreed to U.S. President Donald Trump's request to release diesel reserves. Crude oil prices settled lower after the Group of Seven nations announced the release of diesel and crude stocks to ease surging fuel prices.
International benchmark Brent crude futures slipped 6 cents to close at $102.25 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude slid $1.76 to $91.11 a barrel.

The G7 will release 100 million barrels of reserves over the next four months "with a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days," the group's leaders said in a joint statement. The G7 includes France, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the U.S.
Despite the G7 announcement, Brent crude remains above $100 a barrel, up from about $73 before the Iran war started in late February.

The Iran war has also delayed the group's output capacity review — crucial to determine members' 2027 output quotas — because it has thrown estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, industry sources told Reuters last week.
OPEC+ has been raising output targets for much of 2026 after years of production cuts, but most of the increases stayed on paper because of the Middle East conflict.
The seven core OPEC+ members pumped 25 million barrels per day in August, up 630,000 bpd from July, yet still roughly 5 million bpd below prewar levels in February, OPEC data shows.

OPEC+ still has about 2 million bpd of output cuts in place covering most members. It needs the result of the capacity review to decide how to distribute increases, and any changes to output are unlikely before 2027, sources have said.
A separate OPEC+ ministerial group, the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee, which does not set policy, also met on Sunday to review the market.

Though smartphones and wearable devices like fitness bands can accurately tell time, many people still prefer using traditional watches whether for convenience, aesthetics or an appreciation of a well-constructed analog device. In fact, though the luxury market has been in a bit of a slump, watches are a big industry, with a global market exceeding $135 billion and annual growth projections exceeding 5.6%, according to the data aggregator Statista.

A watch can convey status or accessorize an outfit, but they're also popular as collectibles. For beginners, watch collecting is best treated as a hobby first: Most watches lose value, while those that do appreciate can be difficult to identify and buy at retail.
CNBC recently spoke with experts in the business to find out what a beginner might want to consider when starting a watch collection.
Start collecting for love, not for investment returns

First and foremost, building a collection because you enjoy the looks, mechanical details or history of watches can be satisfying. Collectibles are also becoming more accepted as an alternative investing asset class. But experts advise that you aren't likely to outperform more traditional investments.

Charles Tian, the founder and CEO of WatchCharts, a market-research platform that tracks used-watch prices, explained that it's possible to make money buying and selling watches, but collectors are unlikely to beat investments such as an S&P 500 Index over the long term. "I would not get into watch collecting purely from a financial perspective," Tian said.

He noted, however, that desirable watches can still appreciate over time, pointing out that the Rolex Submariner – a diving-style watch that retails new starting at roughly $10,000 – tripled in value on the secondary market from 2010 to a peak price in 2022 during the Covid-era collectibles boom.

"As a collector and watch enthusiast you'd expect me to say that watches are a great investment, but they mostly aren't," said Mike Johnson, founder of WatchPatrol, a site that aggregates data on the secondary watch market. "The majority of watches depreciate and it's hard to tell which new references will ascend into 'modern classic' territory."
In its index over the past year, quality timepieces such as the Breitling Superocean 42 and the Panerai Luminor GMT both saw material declines in value.
"These are fine watches with shrinking prices, and that's the normal case, not the exception," Johnson said.

There are some exceptions, of course. In special (and exceedingly rare) cases, a watch can appreciate dramatically. For instance, a Rolex Daytona owned by actor Paul Newman, a watch which originally retailed at a price as low as $210 in 1972, sold at auction in 2017 for a then-record $17.8 million.
What makes a watch desirable and what holds value
Many factors affect the desirability of a watch.

While there are roughly 450 Swiss watch brands, sales are concentrated in top brands, including Rolex, Cartier, Patek Philippe, Audemars Piguet, Omega, and Richard Mille, according to an annual report on watchmakers from Morgan Stanley and LuxeConsult.

"Brand reputation will usually be the most significant driver, but rarity, where it was manufactured, and a documented history of ownership are also major factors," said Sean Makovsky, the manager of the luxury division at Max Pawn, a Las Vegas-based pawn broker that deals in watches and other valuables. "Limited editions, retired models or watches tied to significant events tend to attract collectors," he added.

The watch brands experts most frequently cited for appreciating (or at least holding) their value are Rolex, Audemars Piguet and Patek Philippe. Recent prices for new watches from these brands started at $6,200, $11,300, and $18,000 respectively, but pricing in the market is always subject to change and the luxury market can be volatile.
If you can buy a new watch from one of these brands from a certified dealer at retail price, you might be able to sell it immediately on the secondary market for a profit, Tian said.
Johnson said it can be difficult to obtain a hot selling watch from a dealer. "You're on a wait list, and the boutique decides when and whether you get to buy," he explained.

"In general, prices on the pre-owned market are a bit softer than new watches, especially when they are still available," said Robert-Jan Broer, founder of Fratello Watches, an online horology magazine based in the Netherlands. "However, this is not the case for watches that have such a high demand that they can't be easily bought new. Many Rolex sports models, but also watches from Patek Philippe and Audemars Piguet are simply unavailable new because the market is hot for them."

The Swiss brand Vacheron Constantin is also collectible, but generally does not hold value on the secondary market as well as Audemars Piguet, Patek Philippe or Rolex. New prices for a Vacheron Constantin start at $14,300 and the brand appeals to collectors for the beauty and craftsmanship of its watches. The brand also has historic appeal; it was established in 1755 and is the oldest watchmaker in continuous operation.
Some less expensive watches also draw interest from collectors.

Johnson cited vintage Seiko diver watches, Omega sports watches, and modern Tudor watches as decent collectibles. "The discontinued Seiko SKX007 dive watch trades around $257 and creeps up a little every year, which is about as dependable as watch values get at that price," Johnson said. He called out the Hamilton Khaki Field and Tissot PRX as popular entry points for new collectors, with used prices in the range of $400.
Makovsky also cited Hamilton automatic watches along with vintage Bulova Accutrons as offering value and long-term collectability without requiring a substantial investment.

At the other end of the affordability spectrum, Tian said MB&F (Maximilian Büsser & Friends), F.P. Journe, and Richard Mille are collectible brands that can also hold their value. New watches from these brands start at start at $3,300, $15,000, and $120,000, respectively.

Aside from the samples noted above, most watches can be expected to lose value over time. That doesn't mean they can't be collected, just that it might be wiser to buy used. "For most brands, you can get a used watch in great condition, for 40-50% off on the secondary market, Tian said.
Buying new or pre-owned watches comes down to circumstances and personal preference.
"Buying new is simple," Johnson said. "You get a warranty, a brand new product, and the satisfaction of being the only person to ever wear it."

"The secondary market is a little more nuanced," Johnson said. "Everything on the used market already has the retail depreciation baked into the price and every single discontinued reference can be found somewhere, if you look hard enough. The trade-offs are real though: no warranty, mysterious service histories, and you have to do your own homework on both the watch and the seller. The money you save buying used could easily be lost to a surprise service or repair bill."

When buying used, it pays to be extra diligent. "Condition is critical," noted Makovsky, "An unpolished case, original dial, matching serial numbers, original bracelet, and complete box and papers can add substantial value. In many cases, two seemingly identical watches can differ in value by thousands of dollars simply because one is completely original and the other has replacement parts or has been over-restored."
Additional costs, mechanical issues, and scammers

Though there are digital watches that people collect and trade — such as the Casio G-Shock, which ranges in price from $40 to $80,000 — most high-end collectible watches are mechanical and operate through the complex interplay of tiny gears, forks, levers and springs. These wear out with regular use. A mechanical watch typically needs servicing every seven to 10 years, according to the experts, and cost depends on the brand, type and model of watch. This can be as low as $200-300, but more expensive watches, or those with mechanical complications such as dials for power-reserve, dates or the phases of the moon can cost thousands of dollars for one service or repair.

"Repair costs as such are hard to predict," Broer said. "If it needs a new crystal, winding crown, etc., the prices are fairly low. But if there's something wrong with the mechanism inside, or a special dial is cracked or damaged, it can become very expensive."

Proper storage is an essential part of protecting and preserving a luxury watch collection. "Watches should be kept in a dry, secure environment away from magnets, excessive humidity, and extreme temperatures, all of which can negatively affect their performance and long-term condition," Makovsky said. "A high-quality safe provides both security and a stable environment for most collections. For particularly valuable collections, professionally managed vault storage may be appropriate, offering an added layer of protection against theft, damage, and environmental risks."

Equally important is preserving everything that came with the watch. "Original boxes, warranty cards, certificates, manuals, hang tags, receipts, and service records should be kept in excellent condition and stored safely," Makovsky said, noting that a complete set of original packaging and documentation can significantly increase a watch's value.
Finally, look out for shady business practices or outright scams when buying or selling a watch.

"Where there's money to be made, there are crooks," Broer said. He said it's important to deal with trusted sources, including authorized dealers and brand boutiques. He noted that collectors can look into the reputation of those they deal with through word of mouth or when these companies have a good rating on watch marketplace sites, such as Chrono24.
"Outright fakes are the famous problem, but the sneakier one is the 'franken-watch'," Johnson said.

He explained that some dishonest sellers will combine components of different watches together and try to sell it as all-original. Other issues are scratched, damaged, or overly polished watches sold as mint, sellers who disappear after receiving payment, and shill bidding at online auctions.
"Even a completely genuine watch can come attached to a dishonest deal," Johnson said. "The defense is to use common sense: buy the seller before you buy the watch."
He also recommended that watch enthusiasts use payment methods with recourse, insist on original photos and serial numbers, and get anything expensive authenticated by an independent watchmaker.

In his 1979 book The Question of Palestine, Edward Said, the Palestinian writer and academic, frames the relationship between Palestinians and Zionists as a “contest between an affirmation and a denial.” Making sense of it requires us to “understand what the instruments of this contest were, and how they shaped subsequent history so that this history now appears to confirm the validity of the Zionist claims to Palestine, thereby denigrating the Palestinian claim. In other words, we must understand the struggle between Palestinians and Zionism as a struggle between a presence and an interpretation, the former constantly appearing to be overpowered and eradicated by the latter.”

To criticize the popular interpretation of Zionism, to frame Israel as a settler-colonial project and to recognize the humanity and history of Palestinians was — and, unfortunately in the Western world, often remains — a radical thesis.

In the new documentary Edward Said: Between Worlds, Danish filmmaker and producer Maiken Baird explores, among other things, how the publication of this book and Said’s consistent advocacy for Palestinian self-determination made him both a model of intellectual integrity and an enemy of the United States. The doc carries the legacy of other Said film projects, including Mike Dobbs’ Edward Said: The Last Interview, released in 2004, but Between Worlds still offers a useful political education. Through impressive archival footage (interviews and lectures, home videos and family photos), Baird, who executive produced Icarus and Orwell: 2+2=5, revives the voice of a crucial public figure and indicts the U.S. and its mainstream media outlets for the role they have played — and continue to play — in abetting the annihilation of Palestinians. She wraps these major themes in a poignant narrative about how Said, exiled from Palestine and alienated from his Arab identity, eventually found his way back to both.

Between Worlds, still seeking distribution following well-received showings at the Toronto and New York film festivals, opens with an audio compilation of news anchors describing Said. They refer to him as a Palestinian activist, and remark on his eloquence in a subtle nod to the way he defies the expectations of a public taught to dehumanize Arabs. In one early clip, Said says he would “like to be identified as a professor of literature at Columbia University.” A voice off-camera repeats the title, with an interrogative intonation, and Said responds with humorous exasperation: “That’s right. I mean that’s what I do for a living.” This moment captures a tension that Said faced in battling assumptions that deep political engagement somehow foreclosed the possibility of other interests.

The beginning of Between Worlds functions as a kind of prelude, offering a straightforward primer on Said. Using the scholar’s own words, Baird lays out Said’s role in public life and defines one of his principle intellectual projects. “Whenever there is a Palestinian effort to tell a story, to put in a dramatic and realizable way the story of Palestine, it’s been assaulted and stopped,” he says in voiceover. “So we appear as if we are orphans, as if we have no origins, we have no narrative as a people. We are being told in a certain sense that we don’t really exist.”

A violent estrangement from land, history and culture defined Said’s early years. Between Worlds smartly shapes itself around Said’s intellectual ideas without giving up the ease of a chronological timeline. After the intro, Baird introduces Said’s interest in memory and who gets to define history, focusing on the scholar’s early years. Said was born into a middle-class family in Jerusalem, Palestine, in 1935. In 1947, he and his family moved to Cairo, ahead of the 1948 mass expulsion of Palestinians from Israel widely known as the Nakba. Through archival interviews, Said explains how his parents rarely talked about their home country except when vaguely citing what they lost. As a result, Said grew up rather politically disengaged and with no real connection to his identity.

Despite not having the language for it, the young Palestinian understood his position as a marginalized person very early on. In school, he identified with stories of indigenous Americans and Black people in America, and noticed how much of his education was filled with historical elisions of the harm done to them. Said’s teaching style was informed by this keenness, as he encouraged his students to approach their studies with healthy skepticism and to question historical silences.

When he was further into adolescence, Said was sent to the United States for boarding school, where the severance from his Arab identity was reinforced. He went on to study at Princeton and then Harvard before landing a teaching job at Columbia University. It’s at this institution that Said would go on to formulate his most enduring theses about Arab identity in relation to the West (Orientalism, 1978); Palestinian history and self-determination (The Question of Palestine, 1979); and the afterlives of imperialism (Culture and Imperialism, 1993). It’s ironic that today the university that served as Said’s intellectual home is at the forefront of sanctioning students and faculty advocating for Palestinians.

The most emotionally poignant parts of the film focus on how the intellectual rebuilt his relationship to his Palestinian identity. After he married Mariam, a Lebanese writer and activist, Said traveled to Beirut with her, connected with people involved in the liberation of Palestine, and embarked on an intensive study of Arabic. Through this re-engagement, he began to notice how the Western media participated in disseminating anti-Arab propaganda, and these observations would go on to inspire many of his books.

There’s substantial attention paid as well to Said’s intellectual development after his early writings, notably how he became disappointed with and estranged from Palestinian comrades like Yasser Arafat, who he believed harmfully capitulated to American and Israeli demands. While Between Worlds touches on Said’s evolving politics, particularly his later advocacy for a nation where Israelis and Palestinians could live in equality, it leaves the viewer wanting additional context.

One of the most jarring elements of Baird’s documentary — as with most nonfiction projects about Palestinians released in the last few years — is how much of the language featured in the film echoes the contemporary moment. It can feel uncanny to watch Said, interviewed throughout the 80s, 90s and early 2000s, argue the same issues that are being litigated today. And it’s striking to see how being asked repeatedly to defend Palestinian self-determination wears on the scholar, who also had other intellectual interests. He was a talented pianist, a prolific literary critic and a founder of what we now call postcolonial studies, a multidisciplinary field that examines the cultural, economic and political afterlife of imperialism.

I first learned about Said as an undergraduate studying English literature at Princeton, our shared alma mater. His debut book Orientalism offered me, as well as many others, a renewed understanding of the violent legacy of colonization and reinvigorated my understanding of identity as fluid and relational. If there’s one tension in Between Worlds, it’s the constant reminder that there’s so much more to learn about its subject.

Marjoe Gortner, the celebrity child preacher who was the subject of an Oscar-winning documentary and an actor with roles in Earthquake, When You Comin’ Back, Red Ryder? and Falcon Crest, has died. He was 82.
Gortner died Friday of complications from congestive heart failure, his family announced.

With a contract at Universal Pictures, Gortner made his onscreen acting debut as the junkie Teddy Hopper in the 1973 Joseph Sargent-directed telefilm The Marcus-Nelson Murders, which served as the pilot for the CBS crime series Kojak, starring Telly Savalas.

He had another featured role as Jody Joad, a grocery store manager turned National Guardsman, in the Mark Robson-directed disaster movie Earthquake (1974), and he played a psychopathic, hostage-taking Vietnam veteran in Milton Katselas’ When You Comin’ Back, Red Ryder? (1979).

On the sixth season (1986-87) of the CBS primetime soap opera Falcon Crest, Gortner drew on his real-life experience to portray Vince Karlotti, a colorful polygamist and faux psychic medium over 17 episodes.

Hugh Marjoe (a combination of Mary and Joseph) Ross Gortner was born on Jan. 14, 1944, in Long Beach, California. He spoke eloquently as a child, so his parents, Vernon, a Christian evangelical minister, and mother, Marge, had him ordained as a preacher at age 4, when he performed a marriage ceremony for a Paramount newsreel.

Now a celebrity, the long-haired Gortner delivered gyrating, dramatic sermons at revival meetings across the U.S. as his family amassed a fortune estimated to be worth $3 million, but he said his father took off with the money shortly before Gortner turned 16.

He rejoined the ministry as a way to earn a living and in 1971 granted a film crew access to him during his final revival tour. The resulting 1972 documentary, Marjoe, produced and directed by Howard Smith and Sarah Kernochan, debuted at Cannes and won the Oscar for best feature documentary. (The poster called it “a real story millions of people refuse to believe.”)

In the film, Gortner — who said he studied Mick Jagger as a model for his routine — talks about how he and other evangelists manipulated regular folks during revivals, and he’s seen in his hotel room counting the money he had collected one day.

In his review for The New York Times, Vincent Canby described the film as “less a documentary about Marjoe’s final weeks on the Pentecostal church-and-tent circuit than a feature-length screen test for a career in show biz.”

In 1972, Gortner recorded an album, Bad, but Not Evil, which featured him singing Bob Dylan’s “I Shall Be Released” and “Lo and Behold!,” and with all this notoriety, he was signed to a contract at Universal.
Gortner also starred with Lynda Carter in Bobbie Jo and the Outlaw (1976), appeared in the daredevil biopic Viva Knievel! (1977) and toplined a low-budget space opera, Starcrash (1978).

His résumé included appearances on Barnaby Jones, Medical Center, Police Story, Laugh-In, The A-Team, Fantasy Island, Airwolf and Hotel, and he played a preacher in Wild Bill (1995), one of his final roles.
He also produced Circus of the Stars specials and celebrity sports invitationals that helped raise money for charity.

Survivors include his fifth wife, Susan, whom he married in 2019. He was briefly married to American Graffiti actress Candy Clark — they starred together in When You Comin’ Back, Red Ryder? — in the late ’70s.

Ed Sheeran enlisted a familiar face as a surprise opener for his Loop Tour stop in Atlanta.

During his Saturday (Oct. 3) concert at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, the English singer-songwriter welcomed Isaac Slade, the former frontman of The Fray, as a special guest to perform an abbreviated set before Sheeran took the stage.
Slade performed The Fray’s “How to Save a Life” and “You Found Me” while also addressing the war in Gaza and urging the audience to seek common ground amid the polarization surrounding the conflict.

“Everybody seems to be taking sides in this world and that’s good,” Slade told the crowd in fan-captured video. “What’s happening over there [in Gaza] is wrong but if we’re going to get through it, we’re going to need people to step into that middle place, that common ground.”

The singer continued, “That bonfire in the middle of the field that sees both sides, that understands that peace is not a lack of conflict. Peace is not a blank canvas that we need to guard and be polite.”
“[Peace] holds enough beauty, enough tragedy, enough sorrow, enough joy and life if we learn how to integrate it and hold each other in balance. We will find a way through this together,” he added.

Slade’s appearance came amid the fallout from the removal of Sheeran’s previous opening act Macklemore from the U.S. leg of the tour. The “Thrift Shop” rapper took the stage at Sheeran’s Sept. 4 and 5 shows at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium, where he performed “Hind’s Hall” and called for a “Free Palestine.”

Macklemore was scheduled to open several remaining Loop Tour dates, including Saturday’s show in Atlanta. Sheeran later said the decision to remove him was made by the tour’s promoter after venues indicated they would not allow the shows to proceed with Macklemore on the lineup.
Following Macklemore’s removal, the other scheduled supporting acts — Aaron Rowe, Finneas and Lukas Graham — withdrew from the tour. Sheeran’s backing band, Beoga, also departed.
Since leaving Sheeran’s tour, Macklemore has launched his own headlining Free Palestine Tour, with dates already sold out.

Sheeran subsequently performed his Sept. 19 show in Philadelphia without an opening act. During the concert, he addressed the controversy and said he wanted his shows to focus on “love, hope and unity,” while also acknowledging the suffering in both Israel and Gaza.

Slade previously joined Sheeran onstage during the singer’s Loop Tour stop in Toronto in August, where they performed “How to Save a Life.” Sheeran told the audience he had been a fan of Slade’s music and songwriting during his formative years as a teenager.
